name: quaich
author: notation (invented notation / mini-language direction)
description: PRIVATE. NESTING CUPS. Three colours of cup: R, G, B. A cup can only be closed by a cup of one specific other colour, and the closing relation is a 3-cycle -- R is closed by G, G is closed by B, B is closed by R (D = {'R':'G','G':'B','B':'R'}). There are no shapes that only open or only close: every colour can do both. A row of cups is STACKABLE if the eager left-to-right reading empties a stack: take the next cup, and if its colour closes the cup currently on top, snap that pair shut (pop), otherwise put it on top (push). It is ONE SINGLE TOWER (whole) if the stack is empty only after the very last cup -- no proper prefix closes -- i.e. the answer is one nest of cups inside cups, not two towers standing side by side. Equivalently a tower is a tree of boxes whose walls are a pair (t, D[t]) and where a box of colour t may only hold boxes of colour t or P[t] (P = cyclic predecessor); the eager reading is what forbids a child starting with D[t] (it would snap the parent shut early). CLUE: a jumbled pile -- a scrambling of the cups of some single tower of 12/14/16/18 cups (all three colours present, each at least twice) which is itself NOT stackable. ANSWER: any arrangement of exactly the same pile of cups that is stackable and is one single tower. The scorer reads ONLY the letters R/G/B in the answer, in order, and ignores every other character, so the answer may be sent as a bare word or as a drawing; solve() always returns the DRAWING -- nested ASCII boxes, one box per pair, opening colour on the top edge, closing colour on the bottom edge -- so that the demo is a picture of nested boxes rather than a stroke string. INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH: (1) the answer uses exactly the cups of the clue (an anagram); (2) each box in the picture has two different colours, and always the same pair R/G, G/B, B/R -- so each colour is closed by one specific other colour; (3) the drawing is one single outer box (top-level concatenation is forbidden -- two towers side by side score 0, and this clause costs a demo because RG|GB style pair-chains look right); (4) the hidden layer, NOT visible in the picture, is the eager reading: a box may only hold boxes of its own colour or of the previous colour in the cycle, because a child starting with D[t] snaps the parent shut early. WITNESSES CLOSED (measured over 500 clues, all 0/500): empty string, the clue itself (guaranteed unstackable by generate), any constant answer, sorted order in all three rotations, descending order, reversed clue, palindrome (half+mirror), greedy pair-concatenation RG*a GB*b BR*c. A uniformly random shuffle scores 1.0%. Only the real rule gets above a few percent. solve() builds a RANDOM tree (shape and child order seeded by the clue), never a canonical fully nested tower, so demos do not hand over a template. ITERATION 1 (v1, stroke skin '/ - |', run lab-quaich-1, 2 Opus players): MIXED / on target for AI balance -- quaicha CRACKED (final 3539/3539) at round 5-6 on 3 demos, quaichb PARTIAL (728/3149 = 23%), mean 64%. But the 12-year-old judge scored v1 1.6/5: no recognisable object, abstract stroke grammar, nameable as 'custom bracket matching'. ITERATION 2 (this file) is a pure RE-SKIN for kid-legibility: the alphabet / - | is relabelled R G B and solve() draws the answer as nested boxes. Verified: generate(seed) is exactly the relabelling of v1's generate(seed) for all seeds tested, and score() agrees with v1's score on 10000 random relabelled probes, so the clue distribution and the accepted set are isomorphic to v1 and v1's balance evidence carries over unchanged. OPEN WITNESS FAMILY (deliberately left open, unchanged from v1): quaicha never found the nesting or the eager reading but recovered the pair-count decomposition -- with a=#G, b=#B, c=#R it computes p=(a+b-c)/2, q=a-p, r=b-p and emits a fixed three-block layout with case splits for r=0, q=0 and for a first block longer than the last; verified 500/500 against this scorer. It is an earned construction (it needs the discovery that each colour pairs with one specific other colour) and measured attempts to close it are not worth it: a 'no run of k identical cups' clause removes 54% (k=3) / 14% (k=4) of the accepted set while still leaving the family valid on 20% / 51% of clues; a 'some box holds >= 2 boxes' clause does not separate (83% of the family vs 99% of random valid towers). Closing it properly needs positional information in the clue (the hole-completion variant, idea 6 in NOTES_notation.md), i.e. a different challenge. KNOWN RISK of this version: the picture makes clauses (2) and (3) visible in demo 1, which v1 hid, so AI players should get the pairing and the wholeness clause faster; only the eager-reading layer stays hidden. Expect the mean final rate to rise; if the next run comes back too_easy the compensating lever is the depth-parity twist (idea 9: the closing relation runs the other way round the cycle at odd depth), which stays kid-visible in the same drawing.
solve:
D = {"R": "G", "G": "B", "B": "R"}          # a cup of colour t is closed by D[t]
P = {"R": "B", "G": "R", "B": "G"}          # cyclic predecessor


def solve(clue):
    """Stack the loose cups of the clue into one single nested tower, and draw it.

    Counts of R, G, B force the multiset of nested cup pairs uniquely:
    with p, q, u the counts of R, G, B, there are (p+q-u)/2 pairs (R,G),
    (q+u-p)/2 pairs (G,B) and (u+p-q)/2 pairs (B,R).  Any such multiset can be
    laid out as a tree in which a cup of colour t may only hold cups of colour
    t or P[t].  Tree shape and child order are randomised (seeded by the clue)
    so demos never show a canonical layout.  The tower is then DRAWN as nested
    ASCII boxes -- one box per pair, its opening colour on the top edge and its
    closing colour on the bottom edge -- and the drawing is the answer.  The
    scorer reads only the colour letters, so the plain word is accepted too.
    """
    r = random.Random(clue)
    p, q, u = clue.count("R"), clue.count("G"), clue.count("B")
    a, b, c = p + q - u, q + u - p, u + p - q
    if min(a, b, c) < 0 or a % 2 or b % 2 or c % 2:
        return ""
    cnt = {"R": a // 2, "G": b // 2, "B": c // 2}
    root_t = None
    for t0 in "RGB":
        order = [t0, P[t0], P[P[t0]]]
        seq = [cnt[t] for t in order]
        if seq[0] == 0:
            continue
        zero = False
        good = True
        for v in seq:
            if v == 0:
                zero = True
            elif zero:
                good = False
        if good:
            root_t = t0
            break
    if root_t is None:
        return ""
    order = [root_t, P[root_t], P[P[root_t]]]
    typ = [root_t]
    kids = [[]]
    for gi in range(3):
        g = order[gi]
        prevs = order[gi - 1] if gi else None
        for j in range(cnt[g] - (1 if gi == 0 else 0)):
            cand = [i for i in range(len(typ)) if typ[i] == g or typ[i] == prevs]
            u2 = r.choice(cand)
            typ.append(g)
            kids.append([])
            kids[u2].insert(r.randint(0, len(kids[u2])), len(typ) - 1)

    def word(i):
        return typ[i] + "".join(word(j) for j in kids[i]) + D[typ[i]]

    def draw(i):
        ins = []
        for j in kids[i]:
            ins += draw(j)
        w = max([len(x) for x in ins] + [3])
        out = ["+" + typ[i] + "-" * (w + 1) + "+"]
        for l in ins:
            out.append("| " + l + " " * (w - len(l)) + " |")
        out.append("+" + "-" * (w + 1) + D[typ[i]] + "+")
        return out

    pic = "\n".join(draw(0))
    return pic if len(pic) <= 1000 else word(0)
